answer: The premise is incorrect. The node2vec paper (Grover & Leskovec, 2016) does not use the Les Misérables network to evaluate link prediction. That network (77 nodes, 254 edges, character co-appearance co-occurrence) appears in the paper only as a qualitative illustration. It shows how the return parameter p and in-out parameter q shape embeddings, with BFS-like exploration capturing structural equivalence and DFS-like exploration capturing homophily/community structure. Node2vec's link prediction experiments used other datasets, mainly Facebook, Protein-Protein Interaction (PPI), and arXiv collaboration networks (e.g., GrQc/ASTRO-PH). Their evaluation held out a fraction of edges as true positives and sampled non-edges as negatives, then scored them with binary operators (Hadamard, average, L1, L2) over the learned embeddings. Les Misérables is therefore not ideal for testing true and false edges: it is small, it has no held-out or labeled edge split, and it is a single weighted co-occurrence graph, so it is useful for visualization rather than link prediction benchmarking.
confidence_reasoning: I'm fairly confident from memory that node2vec used Les Misérables only for visualization and that its link prediction datasets were Facebook, PPI, and arXiv, though I cannot verify exact details of the paper's figures here.
